title: Why Your API Responses Should Be Cacheable
body:
Every time a client requests data your server has already computed, you're paying a cost you didn't have to pay. HTTP caching exists precisely to eliminate that waste, yet it remains one of the most underused tools in a backend engineer's toolkit.

At its core, caching relies on two headers doing complementary jobs. Cache-Control tells the client (and any intermediary proxy) how long a response can be reused without checking back with the server — a max-age of 300 means "trust this for five minutes, no questions asked." ETag, by contrast, gives the response a fingerprint. When the cache expires, the client can send that fingerprint back in an If-None-Match header; if nothing has changed, the server replies with a lightweight 304 Not Modified instead of resending the full payload.

The two mechanisms solve different problems. Cache-Control avoids the network round trip entirely for a while. ETag keeps that round trip cheap once it does happen, since a 304 costs a fraction of a full response. Used together, they let a well-designed API serve the same data thousands of times while doing the real work only once.

The catch is that caching is easy to get subtly wrong: caching a response that changes per-user, or forgetting to invalidate a cache when the underlying data changes, turns a performance win into a correctness bug. Treat cache headers as part of your API contract, not an afterthought bolted on at the edge.
